report.source_text: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed the absence of most of the neck, body, and tail of the pancreas (Figs. 1 and 2), and these findings were further confirmed by magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI). However, the pancreatic head was not enlarged (Figs. 3 and 4). Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) revealed the absence of the dorsal pancreatic duct (Fig. 5). There was no evidence of chronic pancreatitis or other visceral malformations.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 23-year-old Chinese woman presented with incidental hyperglycemia (fasting 12.29 mmol/L, postprandial 22.3 mmol/L) detected on routine school blood test 3 days prior to evaluation. She was asymptomatic with no history of gastrointestinal symptoms, diabetes, or family history of pancreatic disease. Initial laboratory evaluation revealed severely reduced C-peptide levels across all time points (0.621–0.878 ng/mL; normal 1.1–4.4 ng/mL), indicating markedly impaired endocrine pancreatic function. Negative autoimmune markers (anti-insulin, anti-islet cell, anti-GAD antibodies) ruled out type 1 diabetes. Normal amylase and lipase levels suggested preserved exocrine function. MRI with MRA and DWI confirmed the diagnosis by demonstrating absence of the neck, body, and tail of the pancreas with a non-enlarged pancreatic head. MRCP revealed absence of the dorsal pancreatic duct. No chronic pancreatitis or other visceral malformations were identified. Insulin replacement therapy was initiated at up to 45 U daily with good glycemic response. The patient subsequently developed diabetic retinopathy requiring ophthalmology referral.
